bridges.mechanism: A sustained spike in cross‑border missile and drone strikes raises insurance premiums and perceived transit risk for global shipping, prompting tanker operators to reroute or idle vessels and insurers to restrict cover for certain Gulf transits, which lowers crude throughput through key chokepoints.

Higher strike rates create acute operational demands (targeting, ISR, EW) and rich real-world data/feedback that drive defense labs and contractors to shorten iteration cycles and prioritize rapid model improvements, accelerating development velocity for relevant capabilities.

Acute spikes in cross-border strikes that damage ports, energy nodes or logistics hubs produce abrupt cross-asset risk‑off flows and forced reallocations that overwhelm dealer capacity and liquidity in the Treasury market, producing order imbalances and disorderly price moves.

An uptick in defensive resupply (accelerators, electronics, logistics) consumes constrained global manufacturing, testing and shipping capacity and component inventories, crowding out delivery slots and inputs available for commercial AI hardware.

A surge in military resupply shipments to Europe and adjacent theatres consumes container, roll‑on/roll‑off and air cargo capacity and creates input shortages, prompting North American firms to accelerate near‑sourcing and relocation of production away from exposed foreign suppliers.

Sustained increases in defensive materiel resupply funded by Western governments raise expected Treasury issuance or Treasury/Fed support needs, prompting higher rates of long‑maturity bond purchases or other yield‑smoothing interventions to absorb supply and cap yields.

Degradation or diversion of logistics capacity tied to the conflict (fewer vessels, congested air cargo, redirected freight) raises transport costs and lead times, reducing the volume of time‑sensitive cross‑border shipments between the US and Canada.

Improved logistics throughput in the theatre reduces the probability and magnitude of commodity and supply shocks transmitted to global markets, thereby lowering sudden risk‑off episodes and liquidity strains that create stress in the Treasury market.

Rising escalation pressure in the Russia–Ukraine theatre forces Western naval/air assets and political attention toward Europe, reducing deterrent presence in the Gulf and creating opportunities for regional actors and proxies to intensify maritime harassment and limited strikes, increasing regional military escalation.

As escalation pressure around Ukraine rises, policymakers expand sanctions focus and banks increase de‑risking to avoid secondary exposure, causing correspondent banks and trade‑finance providers to curtail services for counterparties linked to Iran/Gulf trade and thereby reducing trade finance availability.

Rising escalation raises perceived geopolitical and sanction risks for investors and corporates (especially for cross-border tech deals), triggering risk-off behavior and postponement/cancellation of AI funding and capex into exposed firms and regions.

Heightened escalation leads governments to impose export controls, procurement preferences and industrial subsidies that disproportionately benefit large incumbent providers able to comply with security vetting and scale, increasing concentration among a few dominant AI vendors.

Rising systemic escalation pressure increases the risk of broader energy and commodity disruptions and a higher term premium (through inflation expectations and geopolitical risk), which raises market‑determined long‑maturity yields.

More effective extraterritorial/secondary pressure constrains suppliers and maintenance providers for Western-made radars, sensors and spare parts, degrading operational performance and readiness rates of deployed air‑defence systems in the Ukraine theatre within procurement and repair cycles.

More effective extraterritorial/secondary measures force component suppliers, logistics firms and banks to cut or block shipments to sanctioned intermediaries and their ecosystems, directly reducing the volume of AI accelerators and boards that reach global markets.

An increase in the effectiveness of extraterritorial/secondary pressure on third‑party firms pushes the targeted government (or its trading partners) to accelerate reciprocal trade measures to shield domestic companies and signal political resistance.

Reduced availability of trade finance and letters of credit directly delays or cancels payments for interceptors, munitions and contracted deliveries, slowing the flow rate of defensive materiel into the Ukrainian operational theatre.

A tightening of trade finance and correspondent banking for affected trade lanes raises transaction costs and payment risk for cross‑border deals, causing investors and foreign corporate buyers to delay or withhold capital allocations into AI hardware manufacturing and startups that rely on those imports.

A drop in availability of trade finance for shipments tied to the Gulf prompt firms to speed up re‑sourcing and relocating production to jurisdictions with more reliable payment/credit channels, raising the observed reconfiguration rate (and conversely, higher availability slows reconfiguration).

Disruptions or slowdowns in crude transit through key chokepoints increase maritime congestion, freight rates and marine insurance costs, delaying and economically constraining shipments of heavy/urgent AI hardware and components to global customers.

Higher crude throughput through key routes eases global shipping congestion and insurance premiums, lowering transport and input costs and supporting larger US–Canada trade volumes; the reverse occurs when throughput falls.

A sudden drop in crude throughput through Gulf chokepoints sharply raises global oil prices and inflation expectations, which directly lifts term premia and pushes up long‑maturity government bond yields.

Rising regional military intensity prompts multinational customers and cloud providers to shift procurement toward fewer geographically secure and politically aligned suppliers, advantaging large incumbents and increasing concentration in AI hardware, cloud and foundational model provision.

Rising military intensity in the Gulf raises disruption risk and insurance/lead‑time uncertainty for globally integrated suppliers, prompting firms to simplify and regionalize production relationships and thereby reduce US–Canada supply‑chain integration.

Escalating military incidents in the Gulf generate abrupt risk re‑pricing and urgent hedging flows that produce liquidity gaps and order imbalances in the Treasury market, increasing observable market stress.

Sustained rises in long-term yields increase borrowing and hedging costs for European purchasers and defense contractors and raise the cash-flow burden on procurement, leading buyers and suppliers to delay or scale back deliveries of defensive systems.

Sustained increases in long-term yields raise the cost of capital and favor large, cash-rich incumbents over smaller, capital-intensive challengers, accelerating M&A and capacity consolidation in AI hardware and cloud services.

Sustained higher long‑term yields increase the cost of financing capital expenditures and inventory for multinational production, leading firms to postpone or scale back cross‑border integration projects and reduce interdependence.

Rising long‑term borrowing costs increase economic strain on exposed domestic industries, which intensify lobbying for protection and induce authorities to introduce reciprocal trade measures at a faster pace.

Increased net purchases of long-maturity Treasuries inject cash into U.S. money markets and ease dollar funding and trade-finance lines, directly enabling faster payments, letters-of-credit and deliveries of defensive systems to Ukraine.

Net purchases of long-maturity bonds (increased intervention flow) inject reserves and lower risk premia, directly easing financing conditions and prompting banks, VCs, and corporates to deploy more capital into AI projects and funds.

A sustained loss of US policy credibility after a Treasury crisis reduces foreign banks' and states' belief in consistent enforcement and political follow‑through, lowering their perceived legal/political risk and weakening the deterrent effect of US secondary measures on commerce with Iran.

A rapid decline in policy credibility raises macro and regulatory uncertainty, increasing required returns and drying up high-risk long-duration funding, causing venture and corporate AI investment to contract sharply.

A collapse in policy credibility raises political pressure on decision‑makers to show decisive action, prompting quicker introduction of visible reciprocal trade measures (tariffs/quotas) to signal responsiveness.

Acute stress in the US Treasury market causes global banks to hoard liquidity and cut non‑core, higher‑risk correspondent and trade‑finance lines (including those that historically dealt indirectly with Iran), directly reducing the availability of letters of credit and correspondent services for Iranian trade.

Systemic bond‑market stress triggers rapid de‑risking by international banks and corporates who seek to avoid any exposures that could attract regulatory scrutiny, thereby making US extraterritorial/secondary measures more effective in curtailing third‑party dealings with Iran.

Acute bond-market stress forces banks and freight financiers to pull or sharply re-price trade-finance, letters of credit and insurance, directly constraining commercial shipping, maintenance and transport throughput that sustain military and civilian materiel flows.

Acute stress in the bond market tightens short-term financing and triggers margin calls for suppliers and distributors, forcing producers to delay shipments or cut production of AI accelerators and boards due to working-capital shortages.

Acute bond‑market stress tightens short‑term funding and trade‑finance lines and forces firms to delay shipments and cut orders, producing an immediate drop in cross‑border goods and services volumes between the two countries.

A tightened global supply of specialized AI accelerators raises dependence on a limited set of compliant vendors and channels, reducing sanctioned actors' ability to procure alternatives and thereby increasing the practical leverage of secondary sanctions.

Tightening of AI-targeted accelerator supply (fewer available GPUs/TPUs) reduces the processing headroom for real‑time sensor fusion and ML-based tracking on fielded air‑defence nodes, lowering detection/engagement success rates.

A sudden tightening in available AI accelerators and boards reduces cross‑border shipments of hardware and completed systems, directly lowering the dollar volume of US–Canada goods trade as buyers defer or cancel orders.

Large inflows into US AI startups finance rapid build‑out of domestic capacity and procurement contracts with US suppliers, prompting Canadian and multinational customers and contract manufacturers to re‑source or relocate production more quickly to avoid losing market access.

Large, rapid inflows into AI equities and startups prompt investors (including foreign holders) to sell long-maturity Treasuries to fund purchases, driving up yields and forcing authorities to increase purchase operations of long-dated bonds to stabilise markets.

When AI production and cloud/model hosting are concentrated in a few vendors/jurisdictions, governments can directly pressure or sanction those suppliers to cut services to third parties, making extraterritorial/secondary measures more effective.

When AI activity and cash reserves are highly concentrated in a few firms, an idiosyncratic shock to one dominant player (sanctions, outage, or large emergency capex) can trigger synchronized large sell orders or margin calls in the Treasury cash and futures market, spiking liquidity stress and disorderly price moves.

Higher applied tariffs on semiconductor, accelerator and server imports raise landed costs and discourage timely shipments and stocking by resellers, directly reducing the market-available quantity of AI-targeted hardware.

A higher applied tariff profile increases expected import prices and inflation pass-through, lifting inflation expectations and the term premium and thereby pushing up long‑term Treasury yields within months.

A rising pace of reciprocal US–Canada trade measures produces political backlash and reduces Ottawa’s willingness to coordinate with Washington on enforcement and information‑sharing for extraterritorial/secondary sanctions, weakening their practical effectiveness against third parties dealing with Iran.

A faster pace of reciprocal trade measures increases policy and exit risk for cross-border AI ventures, prompting LPs and corporates to pull or re-allocate funding away from binational AI projects and startups.

A faster pace of reciprocal trade measures raises policy and counterparty uncertainty and triggers abrupt position adjustments and liquidity withdrawals in Treasury cash/futures markets, increasing observable market stress.

A fall in US–Canada bilateral trade volumes disrupts cross‑border movement of defense components and munitions (including North American production runs and transit routes), directly reducing the throughput of deliveries destined for Ukraine and thus lowering the defensive asset resupply rate.

Reduced US–Canada supply‑chain integration (fewer coordinated production stages and just‑in‑time links) immediately degrades the cross‑border logistics networks and spare‑parts pipelines that carriers and freight forwarders rely on to sustain large outbound shipments to the theatre, lowering overall logistics operational capacity.

Higher bilateral supply‑chain integration supports a wider set of regional suppliers and OEM partnerships, whereas a decline (from trade frictions) forces sourcing to a smaller number of large, vertically integrated global providers, increasing concentration.

Rapid, forced re‑sourcing and factory relocations impose lead‑time, qualification and capacity ramp costs that disrupt procurement and developer access to compute, slowing the cadence of large-scale model training and releases.

nodes.label: Escalating Russia–Ukraine conflict and strain on European air defences
Cross-border strike rate
nodes.description: The frequency and aggregate kinetic intensity (number and destructive power) of cross-border missile and drone strikes over time.

nodes.label: Air-defence inventory
nodes.description: The quantity of operational air-defence launchers, interceptors and associated munitions available for deployment.

nodes.label: Air-defence effectiveness
nodes.description: The probability or rate at which air-defence systems successfully detect, track and intercept incoming aerial threats.

nodes.label: Defensive asset resupply rate
nodes.description: The flow rate of incoming deliveries and field replacements of defensive systems and interceptors into the operational theatre.

nodes.label: Offensive munition stock
nodes.description: The aggregated stock of offensive munitions (missiles, strike drones, warheads) available for launch operations.

nodes.label: Defensive munition consumption
nodes.description: The rate at which defensive munitions and expendable interceptors are expended during defensive operations.

nodes.label: Logistics operational capacity
nodes.description: The capacity and throughput of transport, maintenance and supply chains to move, repair and sustain military and civilian materiel.

nodes.label: Civilian infrastructure damage
nodes.description: The accumulated extent of damage to civilian and economic infrastructure (energy, transport, storage, public buildings).

nodes.label: Energy flow disruption
nodes.description: The degree to which energy production and transit flows are reduced or interrupted relative to normal baselines.

nodes.label: Grain export rate
nodes.description: The flow rate of agricultural commodity exports passing through trade routes and ports.

nodes.label: Political elite cohesion
nodes.description: The degree of unity and alignment among key political and decision-making elites regarding strategy and policy choices.

nodes.label: Escalation pressure
nodes.description: The systemic propensity for conflict widening and intensification driven by reciprocal actions, signaling and thresholds being crossed.

nodes.label: International assistance willingness
nodes.description: The aggregate willingness and political readiness outside actors have to provide military, logistical or financial support.

nodes.label: Airspace surveillance coverage
nodes.description: The spatial and temporal extent of detection, tracking and intelligence sensors covering contested airspace.

nodes.label: Counter-drone capability
nodes.description: The operational capacity to detect, attribute and neutralize hostile unmanned aerial systems across relevant areas.

nodes.label: Public trust in governance
nodes.description: The level of public confidence and perceived legitimacy of governing authorities and their crisis management.

Financial coercion level
nodes.description: Aggregate intensity of economic and financial pressure tools (sanctions, asset restrictions, payment constraints) applied against the target economy.

nodes.label: Sanction scope coverage
nodes.description: Breadth of sanction measures across geographic regions and economic sectors that affect trade and finance channels.

nodes.label: Secondary pressure effectiveness
nodes.description: Effectiveness of extraterritorial/secondary measures in altering third‑party commercial and financial behavior toward the target.

nodes.label: Trade finance availability
nodes.description: Accessibility and capacity of banking, letters of credit, correspondent networks and other payment instruments that enable cross‑border trade in affected commodities.

nodes.label: Crude throughput rate
nodes.description: Rate of crude oil volume transiting key maritime chokepoints and export routes per unit time.

nodes.label: Refined product supply balance
nodes.description: Net balance between available refined fuels (gasoline, diesel, jet) and regional demand, expressed as surplus or deficit.

nodes.label: Tanker capacity availability
nodes.description: Available seaborne transport capacity for crude and refined product shipments relative to logistical demand.

nodes.label: Marine insurance cost
nodes.description: Average premiums and war‑risk surcharges charged to insure maritime shipments through contested routes.

nodes.label: Refinery utilization rate
nodes.description: Percentage of installed refinery processing capacity that is operational and processing feedstock at a given time.

nodes.label: Regional military escalation
nodes.description: Intensity and tempo of conventional and irregular military actions in the region that affect security of trade and infrastructure.

nodes.label: Proxy attack frequency
nodes.description: Rate at which proxy or irregular forces carry out attacks against infrastructure, shipping, or military assets in the operational theater.

nodes.label: Cyber disruption incidence
nodes.description: Frequency and severity of cyber operations that disrupt energy infrastructure, logistics, or trade‑support systems.

nodes.label: Third‑party buyer demand
nodes.description: Level of demand from non‑sanctioning or neutral buyers for the target's commodity exports.

nodes.label: Market price volatility
nodes.description: Degree of short‑term variability and uncertainty in commodity and refined product prices perceived by market participants.

nodes.label: Financial market liquidity
nodes.description: Depth and ease with which financial assets and trade settlements can be transacted without large price impacts in markets relevant to the campaign.

nodes.label: Coalition policy cohesion
nodes.description: Degree of alignment and coordination among relevant governments and policy actors in designing and enforcing collective measures.

Bessent's Treasury Bond Interventions vs. Market (and Fed) Credibility
Long-term yield level
nodes.description: Market-determined average yield on long-maturity bond instruments.

nodes.label: Yield volatility
nodes.description: Short-term variability in long-maturity bond yields measured by price or yield swings.

nodes.label: Market intervention flow
nodes.description: Rate of purchases or sales of long-maturity bonds executed to influence market yields.

nodes.label: Intervention capacity
nodes.description: Available financial resources and operational flexibility that can be deployed to support markets.

nodes.label: Bond market liquidity
nodes.description: Depth and immediacy of tradable orders and bid-ask tightness in the long-maturity bond market.

nodes.label: Liquidity-provider activity
nodes.description: Aggregate quoting and transaction activity by liquidity-providing agents that sustains market execution.

nodes.label: Inflation expectations
nodes.description: Market-implied or survey-based expected path of consumer prices over relevant horizons.

nodes.label: Policy credibility
nodes.description: Market confidence in policymakers' consistency and ability to achieve stated macroeconomic objectives.

nodes.label: Term premium
nodes.description: Additional yield investors require to hold longer-duration bonds versus short-term alternatives.

nodes.label: Debt supply rate
nodes.description: Pace at which long-maturity debt instruments are issued into the market.

nodes.label: Safe-asset demand
nodes.description: Aggregate investor demand for assets perceived as low-risk stores of value.

nodes.label: Currency exchange value
nodes.description: Market valuation of the currency relative to a basket of other currencies.

nodes.label: Alternative safe-asset prices
nodes.description: Price level of non-bond safe assets that respond to shifts in safe-haven demand.

nodes.label: Market sentiment
nodes.description: Aggregate investor risk appetite and willingness to hold duration and credit risk.

nodes.label: Short-rate expectations
nodes.description: Market-implied expected path of short-term interest rates over coming horizons.

nodes.label: Market stress level
nodes.description: Degree of systemic stress in the bond market reflected in liquidity shocks, order imbalances, and disorderly price moves.

nodes.label: Possible tap of Treasury General Account
AI investment and commercialization race with Nvidia at the center
AI compute capacity
nodes.description: The aggregate available specialized compute resources for AI workloads measured as deployable GPU/accelerator hours or equivalent compute throughput.

nodes.label: AI hardware supply
nodes.description: The market-available quantity of AI-targeted hardware (accelerators, boards, racks) that can be procured for training and inference.

nodes.label: Memory chip cost
nodes.description: The unit price level of memory semiconductors used in AI servers and data centers, reflecting cost per gigabyte or similar metrics.

nodes.label: Data center build rate
nodes.description: The rate at which new data center capacity (power, racks, cooling) is being commissioned and brought online.

nodes.label: Model development velocity
nodes.description: The pace at which AI model capabilities and architectures improve, measured by frequency and magnitude of capability gains.

nodes.label: Model pricing pressure
nodes.description: The prevailing upward or downward pressure on the prices charged for model access, API calls, or per-inference billing.

nodes.label: Robotics commercialization rate
nodes.description: The rate at which robotic systems transition from prototypes to revenue-generating, repeatable deployments in real-world settings.

nodes.label: AI capital inflows
nodes.description: The flow of investment capital (VC, private equity, corporate capex) being allocated to AI hardware, models, and downstream commercialization.

nodes.label: Investor sentiment
nodes.description: The collective market perception and risk appetite regarding AI-related firms and valuations, reflected in price-to-forward metrics and willingness to fund.

nodes.label: Market concentration
nodes.description: The degree to which production, sales, or capacity in AI hardware, cloud services, and foundational models are concentrated among a few dominant providers.

nodes.label: Supply chain resilience
nodes.description: The ability of semiconductor and hardware supply chains to absorb demand shocks and sustain production without large delivery delays or shortages.

nodes.label: Geopolitical fragmentation
nodes.description: The extent of cross-border decoupling and trade/technology restrictions that impede integrated global flows of components, skills, and data.

nodes.label: Regulatory scrutiny level
nodes.description: The intensity and pervasiveness of regulatory attention, investigations, and policy interventions targeted at AI-related activities and markets.

nodes.label: Open model proliferation
nodes.description: The rate at which open-source AI models and permissively released model weights and tooling are published and adopted.

nodes.label: Downstream product adoption rate
nodes.description: The speed at which enterprises and consumers incorporate AI-enabled products and services into normal operations and consumption.

nodes.label: Labor productivity shift
nodes.description: The net change in workforce productivity attributable to AI-driven automation, augmentation, and task reallocation.

nodes.label: Rising memory costs / server price hikes
China eases limits on Nvidia H200 chips
Nvidia talks to invest in Perplexity
U.S.-Canada tariff standoff escalating into trade war
Tariff rate profile
nodes.description: The average applied ad‑valorem and specific tariff intensities across goods and services subject to the bilateral dispute.

nodes.label: Retaliation rate
nodes.description: The pace at which new reciprocal trade measures (tariffs, quotas, or targeted restrictions) are introduced over time.

nodes.label: Bilateral trade flow
nodes.description: The volume and value of cross‑border goods and services exchanged per unit time between the two trading partners.

nodes.label: Supply‑chain integration
nodes.description: The degree of cross‑border interdependence in intermediate inputs, production stages and just‑in‑time logistics linking firms on both sides.

nodes.label: Negotiation intensity
nodes.description: The frequency, duration and resource intensity of formal bargaining, talks and mediation efforts aimed at resolving trade differences.

nodes.label: Political risk perception
nodes.description: The perceived likelihood among economic actors that political escalation will disrupt trade relations and commercial operations.

nodes.label: Sectoral exposure index
nodes.description: The aggregated susceptibility of specific industries (autos, metals, agriculture, electronics, etc.) to bilateral trade barriers and shocks.

nodes.label: Production capacity utilization
nodes.description: The operating rate of industrial and manufacturing capacity in sectors affected by the trade conflict.

nodes.label: Consumer price pressure
nodes.description: Upward pressure on consumer prices for goods and inputs resulting from tariffs, supply disruptions, and pass‑through effects.

nodes.label: Capital flow volatility
nodes.description: Short‑term variability in cross‑border portfolio and direct investment flows driven by trade uncertainty and risk repricing.

nodes.label: Exchange rate pressure
nodes.description: Directional and magnitude pressure on the bilateral exchange rate arising from trade imbalances, capital flows and policy responses.

nodes.label: Market disruption expectation
nodes.description: The market‑implied probability and horizon of persistent trade disruption as reflected in asset prices and risk premia.

nodes.label: Legal dispute activity
nodes.description: The rate of initiating trade remedy actions, filings, arbitrations and administrative legal challenges related to the dispute.

nodes.label: Supply reconfiguration rate
nodes.description: The speed at which firms re‑source inputs, relocate production, or reroute logistics to mitigate tariff exposure.

nodes.label: Labor market disruption
nodes.description: The extent and persistence of employment shifts, layoffs, and wage pressure in industries directly affected by trade measures.

nodes.label: Multilateral rule power
nodes.description: The effective strength and enforceability of multilateral trade rules and dispute mechanisms that constrain unilateral action.

A rising pace of reciprocal US–Canada trade measures produces political backlash and reduces Ottawa’s willingness to coordinate with Washington on enforcement and information‑sharing for extraterritorial/secondary sanctions, weakening their practical effectiveness against third parties dealing with Iran.

A faster pace of reciprocal trade measures increases policy and exit risk for cross-border AI ventures, prompting LPs and corporates to pull or re-allocate funding away from binational AI projects and startups.

A faster pace of reciprocal trade measures raises policy and counterparty uncertainty and triggers abrupt position adjustments and liquidity withdrawals in Treasury cash/futures markets, increasing observable market stress.

A fall in US–Canada bilateral trade volumes disrupts cross‑border movement of defense components and munitions (including North American production runs and transit routes), directly reducing the throughput of deliveries destined for Ukraine and thus lowering the defensive asset resupply rate.

Reduced US–Canada supply‑chain integration (fewer coordinated production stages and just‑in‑time links) immediately degrades the cross‑border logistics networks and spare‑parts pipelines that carriers and freight forwarders rely on to sustain large outbound shipments to the theatre, lowering overall logistics operational capacity.

Higher bilateral supply‑chain integration supports a wider set of regional suppliers and OEM partnerships, whereas a decline (from trade frictions) forces sourcing to a smaller number of large, vertically integrated global providers, increasing concentration.

Rapid, forced re‑sourcing and factory relocations impose lead‑time, qualification and capacity ramp costs that disrupt procurement and developer access to compute, slowing the cadence of large-scale model training and releases.
